content: Induced abortion can reduce the risk of fetal and neonatal mortality. It also eliminates the potential risk of viral persistence in pregnancy-related fluids and tissues. However, induced abortion may conflict with the beliefs, values, or legal and policy frameworks of certain individuals or communities. Performing an induced abortion requires additional resources, including medications like misoprostol (which is low-cost), the use of an Ebola Treatment Center (ETC), full personal protective equipment (PPE) for delivery, and trained healthcare personnel to carry out the procedure. While feasible due to the availability of necessary medications, induced abortion is resource-intensive because it must occur in an ETC with full PPE and trained healthcare workers present. The risk of Ebola virus (EBOV) transmission in pregnant EVD survivors is a critical concern. Evidence suggests that EBOV RNA can persist in pregnancy-related fluids and tissues, and the virus has been isolated from fetal tissue in some cases, indicating potential ongoing infectivity. The findings are limited by the small number of studies, study design quality, and potential reporting bias. Among breastfeeding women with acute or convalescent EVD, there is a suspected high risk of viral transmission through breast milk, which may persist for over a month after symptom onset. Viral persistence and successful isolation of the virus from breast milk have been documented. However, small sample sizes and methodological limitations confound the understanding of transmission routes between mothers and infants during breastfeeding. No studies specifically addressed delivery or abortion outcomes in this population. The use of the rVSV-ZEBOV Ebola vaccine in pregnant women exposed to acute EVD or its body fluids has been evaluated. While the vaccine is highly effective in the general population, evidence on its efficacy and safety in pregnant women is limited. One study aimed to assess vaccine efficacy among pregnant women but found no cases of EVD in either the vaccinated or control groups. Safety data are also limited, with no significant increase in pregnancy loss observed among vaccinated women. Regarding teratogenicity, one study found no teratogenic malformations among 38 infants born to vaccinated women, but the study was limited by small sample size and short follow-up duration. The potential benefits of administering the rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine to pregnant women include preventing maternal infection and associated near 100% pregnancy loss or neonatal death in fetuses. It also reduces the risk of transmission to healthcare providers and community members during delivery. However, as a live-attenuated vaccine, it poses a theoretical risk to fetuses, and safety data in pregnant women remain insufficient. Stakeholders may have differing opinions on vaccine administration during pregnancy, and pregnant women or their families may be unwilling to accept the vaccine due to safety concerns. Offering the vaccine aligns with the principle of autonomy, allowing women to make informed decisions. Resource use for administering the vaccine to pregnant women would increase, requiring healthcare workers, vaccine supplies, and associated costs. However, if vaccine administration reduces EVD cases in pregnant women, treatment costs and resource demands would decrease. Offering the vaccine in areas undergoing ring vaccination is feasible and applicable. Evidence gaps remain regarding the safety and efficacy of interventions, maternal and neonatal outcomes, and healthcare worker acceptability. Further research is needed to guide clinical practice and policy decisions effectively.
